decks.title: Write the rule for a three-piece graph (packet + whiteboards)

items.front: Say the frame: Piece ___ is the line with slope ___ on the interval ___, so its rule is ___.
items.back: Piece A is the line with slope 3 on the interval −2 ≤ x < 1, so its rule is 3x − 4.

items.front: Example 3, piece A: points, slope, b, rule?
Piece B: interval, slope, b, rule?
items.back: 1 ≤ x ≤ 5, through (1, 4) and (5, 8): slope 1. 4 = 1(1) + b, so b = 3. Rule: x + 3.

items.front: Piece C: interval and rule?
items.back: 5 < x ≤ 8, flat at y = 8: slope 0, so f(x) = 8.

items.front: Which quiz items does Example 3 feed, and what do they test?
items.back: Q1 and Q3: match a graph to its rule. The choices differ by the slope of a piece and by < vs ≤ at the endpoints. Check each slope, then each circle.

items.front: A board says: "Piece A is −2 ≤ x ≤ 1."
items.back: The point at (1, −1) is open, so x = 1 is not on A: −2 ≤ x < 1. x = 1 belongs to B, where (1, 4) is closed. Each x gets exactly one piece.

items.front: A board says: "Piece C has slope 0, so its rule is 0" (or "x = 8").
items.back: Slope 0 means flat at the height of the piece: f(x) = 8. x = 8 would be a vertical line.

items.front: Interacting, round 1: ?
items.back: Boards: the interval for piece A, −2 ≤ x < 1. Boards up, one board explains with the frame while you write it on the frozen page (minute 3).

items.front: Interacting, round 2: ?
items.back: Slope of piece A from two points: 3 (minute 5).

items.front: Interacting, round 3, then pairs: ?
items.back: Use (−2, −10) to find b = −4, so 3x − 4. Then pairs do B (x + 3 on 1 ≤ x ≤ 5) and C (8), each rule into the packet as it is confirmed (minute 6 to 10).

items.front: Boards go up: what do you say?
items.back: "Boards up, hold them still." Choose one board to explain with the frame; write that step on the frozen board; unfreeze only to turn the page.

items.front: Extending (minute 10): the exit move?
items.back: One student assembles the three rules in case notation at the SMART board; the class copies it. Ask: why x < 1 for A and 1 ≤ x for B? Each x gets exactly one piece.
